The United States also had 190 kt of dc metallurgical-grade silicon (mg-Si) manufacturing capacity, of which 74 kt (or 35.7 GW ) was dc for PV, with the remaining serving semiconductors and other commercial applications. Wafers for cells, glass for modules, and many other subcomponents were almost exclusively imported, mostly from China. Domestically manufactured modules and cells in 2024 were most likely sold for domestic use, while all U.S. polysilicon manufactured for PV was exported to Vietnam, Malaysia, and Turkey as a source of legally compliant polysilicon for products to be sold back to the U.S. market. Most c-Si PV modules installed in the United States in 2024 were bifacial. While global manufacturing has shifted to producing tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) cells (Fischer et al. 2025), most manufacturers importing cells into the United States—and most operational and planned domestic cell plants—produced lower-efficiency PERC cells in 2024, because TOPCon technology faces restrictions due to lawsuits over patent infringement. The direct cost for manufacturing U.S. modules with domestic cells, wafers, and polysilicon is double that of imported modules ($471/kW vs.$229/kW ). While U.S. labor costs are higher dc dc than in competing manufacturing locations, more of the difference is due to higher costs for procuring and shipping other materials and parts from Asia as well as tariffs on those product components and the manufacturing equipment. In particular, the most competitive large-format wafer technologies depend most heavily on Chinese suppliers. Quartz crucibles, diamond wire, and other manufacturing equipment most suitable for PV ingot and wafer production are not widely available outside China. Downstream, screen-printable metallization pastes for cell production are also not widely available outside China. For module assembly, PV-specialized glass, junction boxes, the electrical diodes within junction boxes, and cell stringing, tabbing, and bussing ribbons are not widely available outside China. Manufacturing equipment for ingots, wafers, cells, and modules is also not widely available from U.S. suppliers and is generally lowest cost if sourced from Chinese suppliers. While the United States is developing a local supply chain, it is challenging to achieve the same economies of scale as China. Cadmium Telluride Modules Globally, CdTe modules accounted for 2% of all modules produced in 2024, while accounting for 18% of U.S. PV installations. In 2024, one company (First Solar) was the only large-scale producer of CdTe modules. First Solar began shifting to larger-format, more efficient, and frameless Series 7 modules in 2023. In 2024, more than half its modules produced in the United States were Series 7, while Series 6 (with a bifacial option) constituted 62% of global production. In 2024, there was approximately 22.0 GW of global CdTe module manufacturing capacity dc (8.9 GW domestic) and 15.5 GW of production (6.3 GW domestic). About 5 GW of new dc dc dc dc capacity was ramping up in the United States and India in 2024.
